how-much-to-charge.html.text:
← Mobile detailing bid calculator

How much should I charge for mobile detailing?

A price built from hands-on hours alone prices three-quarters of the job. A three-hour detail with 45 minutes of drive time and 30 minutes of setup and cleanup is really a 4.25-hour stop — about 40% more hours than the hands-on time a quote usually starts from. Every one of those extra minutes is billed time you're not detailing anyone's car, and it doesn't show up unless you put it in the quote.

Open the free mobile detailing bid calculator

What a "$X per detail" price cannot see

Travel, setup, and cleanup. These are hours the customer is paying for even though the polisher isn't running. A stop across town and a stop next door are not the same job at the same price.

Vehicle cost. Round-trip miles at a real per-mile rate — fuel, wear, insurance — are a cost of doing the job mobile, not a rounding error.

Card fees and margin, together. A payment processing fee and a target margin are both slices of the same final price. Priced separately they look small; added together they can claim more of the ticket than either looks like alone.

A bid you can defend

  1. Add hands-on hours, travel hours, setup, and cleanup into one whole-stop hour figure.
  2. Load the wage with payroll burden, then multiply by whole-stop hours.
  3. Add vehicle cost for the round-trip miles, plus supplies and job overhead.
  4. Add the payment fee, then solve for the price that leaves your target margin after all of it.

The calculator does that arithmetic in your browser. It's not a promise of profit or a recommendation to accept a job — it's arithmetic on the numbers you enter, for you to check against your own vehicle, payment, and overhead costs.

Worked example

Three hands-on hours, 45 minutes of travel, 15 minutes of setup, and 15 minutes of cleanup is a 4.25-hour stop for a 3-hour detail. Add 24 round-trip miles at real vehicle cost, $18 of supplies, a $12 overhead allocation, and a 3% card fee, and a $180 quote that looked comfortable against three hours of labor can be a thin margin — or a loss — against the whole stop. The calculator shows the break-even quote and what a target margin actually requires before you promise a price on the phone.

Common questions

How much should I charge for mobile detailing?

Start from the whole stop, not just the hands-on labor: hands-on hours plus travel, setup, and cleanup, times a loaded hourly wage, plus the vehicle cost for the round-trip miles, plus supplies and a card-processing fee if you take cards. A $180 quote that only covers three hands-on hours can still lose money once 45 minutes of driving and 30 minutes of setup and cleanup are added on top.

Why does travel time matter for a mobile detailing quote?

Travel is billed time you are not detailing anyone's car. A 3-hour job with 45 minutes of drive time and 30 minutes of setup and cleanup is really a 4.25-hour stop — about 40% more hours than the hands-on time alone. Quoting off hands-on hours only prices three-quarters of the job.

Do card processing fees actually change what a detailing quote should be?

Yes, and it compounds with margin. A 3% card fee and a 35% target margin are both slices of the same final price, so together they can claim more of the ticket than either looks like alone. Price them as their own lines rather than assuming they come out of "whatever's left."

Common questions

Why is the loaded labor cost $0 on the example, if the example books 3 labor hours?

The example's wage is set to $0 because it models an owner-operator: your own time isn't a separate line item, so the $128.52 contribution on the default $180 quote is your pay plus profit, not profit on top of a paid wage. Enter a real hourly wage here the moment you pay yourself a set rate or hire a second detailer — the burden percent then loads payroll taxes and insurance on top of it the same way it would for an employee.

What is the break-even quote, and how is it different from the target-margin quote?

Break-even is the price that covers direct costs and the payment processing fee with zero contribution left over — on the defaults, $46.08 direct costs ÷ (1 − 3% fee) ≈ $47.51. The target-margin quote in "Price for your target" instead solves for a price where the fee and your target margin together claim their combined percentage of that price — on the defaults, 3% + 35% = 38%, so $46.08 ÷ (1 − 0.38) ≈ $74.32. Quoting at break-even leaves nothing for your time or profit; quoting below it loses money on the job.

What happens if the payment fee and target margin together claim the whole price?

The page flags it instead of printing a number. If fee percent plus margin percent reaches or passes 100%, no price can satisfy both claims at once — the tool shows this as unreachable rather than a negative or infinite "quote," which would read as real advice.

What is the difference between "hourly on hands-on time" and "hourly on the whole stop"?

Hands-on hourly divides contribution by labor hours alone (3 hours on the default job); whole-stop hourly divides the same contribution by every hour the job occupies you — labor plus travel, setup, and cleanup (4.25 hours on the default). The whole-stop number is the one that is actually comparable across jobs with different drive times, since two jobs can pay the same hands-on rate while very different amounts of the day get eaten by travel.

Does the price on this page include a deposit or my business details?

No — deposit percent and hold-days live in the separate proposal section below, which turns the same numbers into a printable quote for the customer. The pricing math above answers "what should I charge"; the proposal section turns that answer into a document with your business details and the customer's, which is only saved on your own device.

Is my pricing or customer information uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculation and the proposal both run in your browser; your saved business details and any usage counts stay in local storage on this device, never sent to a server, and the opt-out checkbox above turns usage counting off entirely.

Hand the customer a proposal

The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

vs-a-flat-per-vehicle-price.html.text:
← Mobile detailing bid calculator

This calculator vs. a flat per-vehicle price card

Names no specific product or company. This compares a free calculator against the generic method every mobile detailer already has: a price card by vehicle size — sedan, SUV, truck — quoted the same regardless of where the job is.

First — the price card is right, and you should have one

A website, a flyer, or a text back to a lead needs one number per vehicle size before you know the address. "$180 for a sedan full detail" is a fine headline price, and no calculator replaces having one. What follows is not an argument that the card is wrong. It is what the same flat number stops showing you the moment the job is real and you know how far it is.

The worked example

Both rows below quote the identical $180 sedan-detail card price from this calculator's own starting numbers: 3 hours of hands-on labor, 25 minutes of setup and cleanup, an owner-operator's own time (wage $0, so contribution is take-home plus profit), $18 of supplies, $12 of job overhead, and a 3% card-processing fee. The only thing that changes between them is the drive.

QuestionNear job — 24 mi round trip, 45 min driveFar job — 60 mi round trip, 90 min drive
What the price card shows $180 — sedan full detail $180 — sedan full detail, unchanged
Round-trip vehicle cost $16.08 (24 mi × $0.67) $40.20 (60 mi × $0.67) — the card never separates this out
Whole-stop time the job occupies 4.25 hours (3 hands-on + 1.25 travel/setup/cleanup) 5 hours (3 hands-on + 2 travel/setup/cleanup)
Card-processing fee $5.40 (3% of $180) $5.40 (3% of $180) — same fee, same price
Direct costs this job actually carries $46.08 (supplies + overhead + travel) $70.20 (supplies + overhead + travel)
Break-even price $47.51 — well below the $180 card price $72.37 — still below $180, but the cushion above it has shrunk
What $180 actually nets after costs and the fee $128.52 — a 71.4% margin $104.40 — a 58.0% margin
Effective hourly on hands-on time alone $42.84 (same 3 hours either way) $34.80 (same 3 hours either way)
Effective hourly on the whole stop $30.24 — what actually fills your day $20.88 — a 31% cut from the near job, at the identical price
Minimum price to still clear a 35% target margin $74.32 — this job's own floor, well under $180 $113.23 — this job's own floor has moved up by $38.91

The two places the price card goes quiet

1. Drive time and drive cost never separate from the job

A price card answers "what do I charge for a sedan," not "what does it cost me to reach this one." Both live inside the same $180 either way. The calculator splits them out — $16.08 of vehicle cost on the near job, $40.20 on the far one — so the card fee, the supplies, and the trip are visible as three separate numbers instead of one guess that happened to work out.

2. The same price pays a falling hourly rate as the drive grows

This is the one that costs real money over a full week. The card charges $180 whether the stop is 12 minutes away or 45, but the hours it occupies are not the same, so the price that felt right on the near job pays 31% less per hour on the far one — $30.24 down to $20.88 — with nothing on the card to say so. A detailer working off the card alone can fill a day with "the same $180 job" and end it having earned noticeably less than the schedule implied, purely from which addresses landed on the route.

When the price card is still the better tool

For advertising, it plainly is. A website or a flyer cannot show a live calculator, and a customer calling for a quote wants one number, not a form. The sensible arrangement is both: post the card price to get the call, then run this calculator once you have the address to see whether that day's version of the job still clears your floor — and, on a job far enough out, whether a trip surcharge or a decline is the honest answer instead.

Every figure on this page is this calculator's own worked example, not a claim about any real detailer or an industry benchmark. Your mileage, rates, and supply cost will produce different numbers — the point is which numbers to produce, not what they should come out to.

Common questions

Is a flat per-vehicle price card wrong?

No, and it should not go away. A website or a flyer needs one number per vehicle size, and "$180 for a sedan full detail" is a perfectly good headline price. The point of this page is not that the card is wrong — it is that the card is the same number whether the job is 5 minutes away or 45, and only one of those two jobs actually clears the margin the card was priced to deliver.

How much does drive time actually cost on a mobile job?

Two things, and a flat card shows neither: the mileage cost of getting there and back, and the clock time it occupies that a shop-based detailer never spends. On this calculator's own defaults, a 24-mile round trip at $0.67 a mile is $16.08 in vehicle cost alone, on top of 45 minutes that never touches the car. Move the same $180 job to a 60-mile round trip and the vehicle cost alone triples to $40.20, before the extra clock time is even counted.

Why does the same flat price pay a different hourly rate on different jobs?

Because the flat price is fixed but the whole-stop time behind it is not. On the near job below, $180 nets $128.52 after costs and the card fee, spread across 4.25 hours the job actually occupies — $30.24 an hour. Charge the identical $180 for a job with double the drive and the net drops to $104.40 spread across 5 hours — $20.88 an hour, a 31% cut the price card never shows, because the card only ever displays the $180.

Does the calculator replace the price card?

No, and it is not trying to. The price card is what you advertise before you know the mileage. This calculator is what you run once you know the address, to decide whether that day's version of "the $180 sedan detail" still clears your target margin — and, if a job is far enough, whether it is worth a trip surcharge or a decline instead.

vs-mobiletechrx.html.text:
← Mobile Detailing Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Mobile Tech RX

Two different shapes: Mobile Tech RX is account-based business management software for running a reconditioning shop's whole marketing-to-invoicing workflow. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one mobile detail cost, given its travel, labor, and supplies, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Mobile Tech RX is web-based business management software built for the auto reconditioning industry — used by businesses across detailing, paintless dent repair, glass repair, paint touch-up, wheel and rim repair, window tint, interior repair, and paint protection film and vinyl. It covers text-message marketing, employee scheduling, estimates, invoicing, and credit-card payment processing, with a QuickBooks integration, and a mobile app for use in the field. It was founded in 2014 by a former paintless-dent-repair technician, later took a Series A funding round led by Silverton Partners, and in 2021 was acquired by AsTech, with an independent trade publication reporting it served roughly six thousand users across the reconditioning industry at the time. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. Mobile Tech RX's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — auto-reconditioning-industry business management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Mobile Tech RX appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Mobile Tech RX does. It does not run marketing campaigns, hold a customer or job record on a server, or manage a schedule across technicians. It takes one mobile detail — hands-on labor hours, travel, setup, and cleanup time, round-trip mileage at your own vehicle rate, hourly wage and payroll burden, supplies and chemicals, job overhead, payment processing fee, and target margin — and turns that into the contribution left after costs, the break-even quote, the price that hits your target margin, the effective hourly rate on hands-on time and on the whole stop, plus a printable customer proposal with scope, deposit split, and a signature line. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
